name: Java
summary: A statically typed, object-oriented language that compiles to portable bytecode for the Java Virtual Machine, with a new release every six months.
intro: The `javac` compiler turns Java source into class files: bytecode and a binary format defined by the Java Virtual Machine Specification, not machine code for one CPU. Any JVM can load the same class files, which is where the old “write once, run anywhere” promise comes from. Memory is managed for you: objects are created with `new`, there is no pointer arithmetic, and a garbage collector frees what is no longer reachable.

OpenJDK, the open-source reference implementation, ships a feature release every six months, in March and September, on a fixed schedule. Vendors pick some releases for long-term support: Oracle’s LTS releases are 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25, and it plans a new one every two years (Java 29 in September 2027). JDK 27 shipped on September 15, 2026.

Since JDK 21 (September 2023) Java has virtual threads (JEP 444): lightweight threads managed by the JDK rather than the operating system. Thousands or millions of them can exist at once, so plain blocking code written one thread per request scales like asynchronous code, without callbacks.
strengths: Compiled class files run unchanged on any JVM, on any operating system and CPU the JVM supports
Garbage collection and no pointer arithmetic rule out whole classes of memory bugs common in C and C++
A predictable cadence: a feature release every March and September, plus long-term support releases for teams that upgrade less often
Virtual threads let simple thread-per-request servers scale to many concurrent requests without rewriting them as async code
limits: A non-LTS release gets only two updates before the next one ships, so you either upgrade every six months or stay on an LTS
Virtual threads add scale, not speed: CPU-bound work runs no faster, and blocking while pinned to a carrier thread can still limit throughput
Generic type arguments are erased during compilation, so code can’t ask at runtime whether a `List` holds `String`s or `Integer`s

snippet.title: Ten thousand blocking tasks, each on its own virtual thread
source: // One virtual thread per task (Java 21+): 10,000 threads are cheap.
Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1));   // blocks only this virtual thread
}   // close() waits for every task to finish
System.out.println("done in " + ms + " ms");   // about a second, not 10,000 seconds

story: In June 1991 James Gosling, Mike Sheridan and Patrick Naughton at Sun Microsystems started a research project to build software for network devices and embedded systems. The goal was a small, reliable, portable platform. They began in C++, but its problems grew until the team decided a new language was the better answer. It was first called Oak, after a tree outside Gosling’s office, and was renamed Java.

Sun released Java in May 1995, and Java 1.0 followed in 1996. Its pitch fit the early web: programs compiled once to bytecode would run on any machine with a Java runtime, at a time when software had to be built separately for Windows, Macintosh and many flavors of Unix. Sun released the JVM and class libraries as free software under the GPL from November 2006 to May 2007, and Oracle took over stewardship when it bought Sun in 2009–10.

Big releases used to arrive years apart, held up by their largest feature. In 2017 Mark Reinhold, chief architect of the Java platform, proposed shipping whatever is ready every six months instead. That model started with JDK 10 in March 2018.

choices.choice: Look like C++, minus its complexity
choices.why: Keeping C++’s syntax and object-oriented feel let C and C++ programmers move over quickly, while dropping features such as pointer arithmetic and manual memory management removed common sources of bugs.

choices.choice: Compile to bytecode for a virtual machine
choices.why: Software had to run on a mix of hardware and operating systems across a network. Machine-independent bytecode, run by an interpreter and runtime on each platform, meant one build could ship everywhere.
A collector running in the background frees memory the program no longer uses, which the designers saw as removing entire classes of errors that troubled C and C++ programmers.
Feature-driven releases slipped while waiting for the biggest feature. A fixed train ships smaller releases on time, and long-term support releases serve teams that can’t upgrade that often.

timeline.text: Gosling, Sheridan and Naughton start the project at Sun as Oak
Sun starts releasing the JVM and libraries under the GPL (finished in May 2007)
Oracle completes its acquisition of Sun and becomes Java’s steward
JDK 10 is the first release on the six-month train
